newsitem.title: UK: Britain seeks to maintain global military role.
newsitem.headline: Britain seeks to maintain global military role.

text.p: After a far-reaching review of Britain's defence needs, the new Labour government has concluded its armed forces should continue to play a global role, Defence Secretary George Robertson said on Wednesday.
"We have to keep a broad balance of capabilities so we can do what the people want us to do. What we have rejected is the idea of minimal defence," he told parliament's defence committee.

Robertson vowed to make military resources, stretched by Britain's peacekeeping duties, go further by overhauling procurement procedures to prevent weapons and equipment being delivered late and over budget.

Soon after taking office on May 1, Labour announced a "strategic defence review". Its opponents charged that the review was an excuse for more deep cuts in military spending in the wake of those imposed by the previous Conservative administration following the end of the Cold War.

But Robertson, writing in Wednesday's edition of the Independent newspaper, said the British public was simply not prepared to retreat into isolationism and watch international aggression like Iraq's invasion of Kuwait in 1991 go unchecked.
He told the committee that Britain needed to maintain its armed forces in a rapidly changing world full of new threats.

"In Europe today, we can see how instability can so easily escalate into major conflict with consequences which spill over borders and threaten our own national security," he said. "Britain cannot be strong at home if it is weak abroad."
Robertson said spending would not be slashed but made it clear the military would have to make better use of its budget.
"The British people want strong defence for this country but they don't want defence at any price and we must justify every pound which is spent in the defence budget," he said.
One method would be to improve weapons procurement, which eats up nine billion pounds ($14.7 billion) of the 22 billion pound annual defence budget.

"It is in the interest of our troops that we liberate money from areas of waste and duplication and put it into the front line," he said, adding that the government would also have to deal with falling troop morale caused by previous defence cuts.
"Just as we've got smart missiles and smart weapons, we need to have smart procurement as well," he said.

"This review is going to include a ruthless examination of how value for money for defence procurement can be improved. I am therefore launching a major initiative to try to eliminate the kind of cost overruns and delays that have characterised some equipment projects in the past."
Robertson said spending on defence as a proportion of national income was already at its lowest level since 1934 and conceded the figure was unlikely to rise.

The defence budget had dropped 23 percent in real terms since the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989 marked the end of the Cold War, even though the tasks facing Britain's armed forces, including peacekeeping in Bosnia, had multiplied.

Roberston said the next phase of the review, perhaps requiring "discomfiting" changes, would look at how the armed forces should be organised to fulfil their tasks. The review should be completed by next February.
